questions.question: What are the three types of changes in ServiceNow?

explanation.correct: There are three types of changes in ServiceNow: Standard (pre-approved, commonly implemented), Normal (requires comprehensive assessments and CAB authorization), and Emergency (must be implemented swiftly, requires ECAB approval). See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: ServiceNow categorizes changes by type, not size.
Internal/External is not the classification used for change types.
These are not the official change type classifications in ServiceNow.

source.excerpt: There are three types of changes. When it comes to service changes, a normal change refers to any change that isn't classified as a standard change or an emergency change.

questions.question: A team has a routine TLS certificate renewal with documented steps and a proven success record. Their change manager wants it raised as a standard change rather than a normal change. What key difference supports this?

options.text: Standard changes skip peer review but still require CAB authorization
Standard changes are pre-authorized and skip group, peer, and CAB approval
Standard changes are reserved for urgent fixes that resolve a major incident
Standard changes require two levels of approval before implementation

explanation.correct: Per the Change types page, a standard change is a pre-authorized, low-risk change that is frequently implemented, has repeatable steps and a proven history of success. Because it is pre-approved, it follows a streamlined process without group-level or peer approval and without CAB authorization, whereas a normal change requires assessment, peer or technical approval and CAB authorization. Routine TLS certificate renewals are the docs' own example of a standard change. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/change-types.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Skipping peer review but still going to the CAB describes an emergency change, which bypasses group and peer review and moves directly to Authorize for CAB approval. Standard changes need no CAB authorization.
Urgent fixes to resolve a major incident or apply a security patch are emergency changes, not standard changes. Standard changes are low-risk, routine, and repeatable.
Two levels of approval (peer or technical approval plus CAB authorization) before implementation is the defining trait of a normal change, not a standard change.

source.excerpt: Changes that are considered standard or pre-approved are commonly put into effect. These changes have a set of established implementation steps and a track record of successful outcomes.

questions.question: What does CAB stand for in Change Management?

explanation.correct: CAB stands for Change Advisory Board. Normal changes require comprehensive assessments and authorizations including peer or technical approval, Change Management, and Change Advisory Board authorization. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: The correct term is Advisory, not Administration.
CAB relates to Change Management, not Configuration.
This is not the correct expansion of CAB.

source.excerpt: Such changes require comprehensive assessments and authorizations, including peer or technical approval, Change Management, and change advisory board authorization.

questions.question: An administrator wants conflict detection to flag any change request planned during the year-end code freeze. Which type of schedule should the administrator create for that period?

options.text: A maintenance schedule covering the freeze
A blackout schedule covering the freeze
An information schedule covering the freeze
A CAB meeting schedule covering the freeze

explanation.correct: Blackout schedules specify times during which normal change activity should not be scheduled, and conflict detection raises a conflict when a change request falls inside a blackout window. The Conflict detection page even gives a year-end code freeze as the example use of a blackout schedule. Conflict detection compares a change's CIs and planned dates against blackout and maintenance windows and other active changes. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/schedule-types-conflict-detection.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A maintenance schedule defines when changes should be scheduled. Conflict detection flags changes that fall outside a maintenance window, so it would not flag changes inside the freeze.
Information schedules record events such as holidays that teams should know about, but conflict detection does not create conflict records for information schedules.
A CAB meeting schedule in the CAB workbench sets up recurring CAB meetings to review changes. Conflict detection does not evaluate it as a change blackout period.

source.excerpt: The Change Management application helps identify schedule conflicts for change requests by analyzing factors such as configuration items, planned start and end dates, and change scope.

questions.question: A requester asks about a normal change that has received final authorization from Change Management and the CAB. Its planned start date is next week, and no work has started yet. Which state is the change request in?

explanation.correct: In the change state model, Scheduled means the change is fully scheduled and authorized and is waiting for its planned start date; an email notification is sent to the requester when the change enters this state. Authorize is the earlier state in which Change Management and the CAB schedule the change and give final authorization, so a change that already has that authorization and is waiting for its window has moved on to Scheduled. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/c_ChangeStateModel.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Implement is the state in which the planned start date has arrived and the actual implementation work is being carried out. No work has started on this change yet.
Authorize is where Change Management and the CAB schedule the change and provide final authorization. Once that authorization is granted, the change moves on to Scheduled.
Assess is where peer review and technical approval of the change details happen. That step comes before CAB authorization, so this change is past it.

source.excerpt: Authorized means that CAB has provided the final authorization to proceed with the change, and we're simply waiting for the scheduled window.

questions.question: Why is it best practice to create emergency changes from an incident?

options.text: To minimize the risk of unauthorized changes by associating with a documented incident
To speed up the approval process automatically
Emergency changes cannot be created any other way

explanation.correct: Emergency changes do not follow the complete lifecycle of a normal change, which can potentially lead to unauthorized changes. To minimize this risk, it is best practice to create emergency changes if they are associated with an incident. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: The main reason is to minimize unauthorized changes, not reduce paperwork.
ECAB approval is still required; linking to incidents doesn't bypass approvals.
Emergency changes can be created independently, but linking is best practice.

source.excerpt: To be implemented swiftly, emergency changes do not follow the complete lifecycle of a normal change, which can potentially lead to unauthorized changes. To minimize this risk, it is best practice to create emergency changes if they are associated with an incident.

questions.question: What are the four types of change tasks in ServiceNow?

explanation.correct: ServiceNow offers four types of change tasks: Planning, Implementation, Testing, and Review tasks. Each task has states including pending, open, in progress, closed, and canceled. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: These are database operations, not change task types.
These are change states, not task types.
These are not the official change task type names.

source.excerpt: ServiceNow offers four types of change tasks-- namely, planning, implementation, testing, and review tasks.

questions.question: An administrator wants database refresh changes to follow their own set of states, state transitions, and approval policies, with fields pre-filled when the request is created. What should the administrator define?

explanation.correct: Change models define the process for a specific change use case. They are built from reusable elements such as change states, change state transitions, approval policies, and change templates, and they can show standard field information when a new change request is created with the model. This tailors a fit-for-purpose process for the use case, so a change model meets every requirement in the scenario. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/manage-change-models.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A blackout schedule sets times when normal change activity should not be scheduled. Conflict detection uses it, but it does not define states, transitions, or approvals.
A standard change template pre-fills pre-approved values for a standard change from the catalog. It does not define its own set of states, transitions, and approval policies.
A CAB meeting agenda uses filter criteria to pick which change requests a CAB meeting discusses. It does not define the process that a change request follows.

source.excerpt: The process details, such as the specific fields, record states, approvals or pre-approvals, and tasks created are determined by the change model and change policies.

questions.question: A change owner runs Check Conflicts on a change request, and the Conflicts tab shows that the CI is already scheduled by another change during the planned window. What is the documented next step?

options.text: Revert the change to New so that the conflicts are cleared
Review the conflicts and reschedule the change to resolve them
Approve the change so that it skips the conflicting time window
Wait for the conflict status to clear in the Scheduled state

explanation.correct: After running conflict detection manually, the change owner reviews the Conflicts Detected list on the Conflicts tab, which shows the conflict type, such as CI Already Scheduled, and any conflicting change. The documented next step is to resolve the conflicts and reschedule the change. The conflict calendar's Scheduling Assistant can help by offering available time slots that avoid the conflict. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/t_RunManualConflictDetection.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Revert to New restarts the workflow and cancels pending approvals. It is meant for adding missing CIs before approval and does not resolve a schedule clash.
Approving a change moves it to Scheduled but does not change its planned dates. The CI would still be scheduled by the other change at the same time.
Conflicts are recalculated when the CI, planned dates, or state change. The overlap stays until the schedule changes, so the owner must reschedule rather than wait.

source.excerpt: It is up to the change owner or the assigned to user to review the conflicts and decide whether to amend the change to avoid conflicts or proceed, anyway. We will constantly update the work notes with the justification if conflicts are ignored.

questions.question: Which methods are available for determining the risk of a change? (Choose two)

options.text: Risk assessments using end-user provided information

explanation.correct: There are two methods for determining change risk: risk conditions (using predefined properties and conditions to calculate a risk value) and risk assessments (relying on information provided by the end user). Both can be used independently or combined, with the highest risk value chosen. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Risk should be calculated systematically, not based solely on personal judgment.
Risk assignment is never random; it follows defined methods.

source.excerpt: To determine the risk of a change, there are two methods available. The first is through risk conditions, which utilize predefined properties and conditions to calculate a risk value. The second is through risk assessments, which rely on the information provided by the end user to assess a risk value.

questions.question: An update set has been marked as 'Complete' but additional changes are needed. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Revert the update set back to 'In Progress' and make the changes
Create a new update set and commit them in the order they were created
Delete the completed update set and start over
Merge the changes directly into the default update set

explanation.correct: Once an update set is marked as complete, don't revert it back to in-progress. Instead, start a new update set and commit them in the order they were created. Use naming conventions like 'Performance Enhancements' and 'Performance Enhancements 2' to keep them organized.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Best practice is to NOT revert a completed update set back to in-progress.
Deleting a completed update set loses the captured changes. Create a new one instead.
The default update set should not be used for moving customizations between instances.

questions.question: How many instances does a ServiceNow customer receive at minimum?

explanation.correct: Customers receive at least two instances: production and non-production. They can add more for tasks like testing, development, or quality assurance.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Customers receive at least two instances, not one.
The minimum is two instances. Additional instances can be added but are not included by default.
Four instances are not the minimum; the minimum is two.

course.lessonTitle: Explore the power of the ServiceNow Platform

questions.question: What architecture does ServiceNow use for its instances?

explanation.correct: ServiceNow uses a multi-instance single-tenant architecture, meaning each instance has its own isolated database. Each instance is hosted at a ServiceNow data center with a unique URL.

wrongAnswers.explanation: ServiceNow is single-tenant (each customer has isolated instances), not multi-tenant.
ServiceNow provides multiple instances per customer (multi-instance) with single tenancy.
Customers receive multiple instances (at least 2), so it is multi-instance.

course.lessonTitle: Explore the power of the ServiceNow Platform

questions.question: A CAB manager wants to set up a recurring weekly CAB meeting, define its attendees, and use filter criteria to pick which change requests go on each agenda. Which feature should the manager use?

explanation.correct: The CAB workbench lets a CAB manager schedule, plan, and manage CAB meetings. It can define a recurring meeting schedule and the attendees for each occurrence, and it uses filter criteria to decide which change requests go on a meeting's agenda. It also provides a change calendar, lets attendees approve or reject changes based on CAB decisions, and records meeting notes. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/cab-workbench.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The standard change catalog lists pre-approved standard change templates that users can request. It does not schedule CAB meetings or build their agendas.
The conflict calendar shows the scheduling conflicts for one change request and offers the Scheduling Assistant. It does not manage CAB meetings or their attendees.
Change approval policies generate approvals by evaluating decisions and approval definitions. They do not schedule recurring CAB meetings or set agendas.

questions.question: When merging multiple update sets, how does ServiceNow handle conflicts where the same object was modified?

options.text: It keeps the latest change to the object
It prompts the admin to choose which version to keep
It creates a new version combining both changes

explanation.correct: When merging update sets, the latest change to an object is kept. This is why it's important to commit update sets in the order they were created.

wrongAnswers.explanation: The merge is not rejected; the system handles conflicts by keeping the latest change.
The system automatically keeps the latest change rather than prompting for selection.
ServiceNow doesn't merge the content of both changes; it keeps the latest one.

questions.question: What are the three types of change in ServiceNow's Change Management? (Choose 3)

explanation.correct: ServiceNow supports three change types: Standard (pre-approved, low-risk, repeatable), Normal (requires assessment and approval through the full change process), and Emergency (fast-tracked for urgent fixes to critical issues).

wrongAnswers.explanation: Cosmetic is not a standard change type in ServiceNow.
Routine is not a defined change type; Standard changes cover pre-approved routine activities.

questions.question: During the Implement state of a normal change, the implementer hits a critical issue and backs out the work, so the change cannot be completed as planned. How should this outcome be recorded?

options.text: Move it to Review and record the outcome in the close code and notes
Use Revert to New so that the change can be resubmitted for approval
Close it with a successful close code so the change metrics stay clean
Change its type to Emergency and send it on to the CAB for approval

explanation.correct: After implementation work ends, the change moves to the Review state. In Review, the change requester decides whether the change was successful, and a post-implementation review can be held. To close the change, the user enters a Close code and Close notes in the Closure Information section, which records the actual outcome. A change cannot be canceled once it is in Review. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/c_ChangeStateModel.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Revert to New is used for Normal changes in Assess or Emergency changes in Authorize when CIs were missed before approval. It does not record a failed implementation.
In Review, the requester determines whether the change was successful. Recording a failed change as successful would make the closure information inaccurate.
A change's Type can be changed only while it is in the New state and before any approvals exist, so a change in Implement cannot be converted to Emergency.

questions.question: A new team member asks what role the Change Advisory Board (CAB) plays in the ServiceNow change process. Which answer is accurate?

options.text: It authorizes normal and emergency changes before implementation
It implements approved changes on behalf of the change owner
It pre-approves each standard change request when it is submitted
It runs conflict detection on every change in the Scheduled state

explanation.correct: According to the Change types page, normal changes need peer or technical approval and CAB authorization before implementation. Emergency changes skip group and peer review and go directly to the Authorize state for CAB approval. CAB meetings are typically used to review and authorize change requests and to review recently implemented changes, so the CAB is an authorization body, not an implementation team. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/change-types.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The CAB reviews and authorizes changes. The actual work is done by the implementer during the Implement state, not by the CAB.
Standard changes are already pre-authorized and need no CAB authorization. Requests created from the catalog skip the Assess and Authorize states.
Conflict detection runs automatically when CIs or planned dates are entered or changed, or it is run manually from the change. It is not a CAB task.

questions.question: Two teams have planned changes on the same server CI for overlapping time windows. The change manager wants this flagged automatically when the CI or planned dates are entered. Which feature does this?

options.text: A UI policy on the change form

explanation.correct: Conflict detection identifies scheduling conflicts from a change's configuration items and planned start and end dates. One reason it flags a conflict is that the CI is already scheduled at the given date and time. It can run automatically when the Configuration item or planned start and end dates are entered or updated, and the results appear in the Conflicts section of the change request. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/it-service-management/change-management/c_ConflictDetection.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: UI policies change form behavior, such as making fields mandatory, read-only, or hidden. They do not compare one change's schedule against other changes on the same CI.
The change risk calculator calculates the risk and impact of a change from defined rules. It does not detect overlapping schedules between changes on the same CI.
Change approval policies generate approvals from decision conditions. They decide who approves a change, not whether its window overlaps another change on the CI.

questions.question: Which statement about Standard changes is NOT correct?

options.text: Standard changes are pre-approved and don't require CAB review each time
Standard changes use templates for consistent implementation
Standard changes require a new risk assessment for every request
Standard changes are low-risk, well-understood procedures

explanation.correct: Standard changes are pre-approved precisely because their risk has already been assessed and accepted. They do NOT require a new risk assessment each time — that would defeat the purpose of pre-approval.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Correct — Standard changes are pre-approved and skip CAB review.
Correct — Standard changes use templates to ensure consistency.
Correct — Standard changes are by definition low-risk and well-understood.

questions.question: Which type of change model in ServiceNow is designed specifically to record change requests from an external system without any associated approvals?

explanation.correct: The Change Registration model is designed to record change requests from an external system without associated approvals, as part of ServiceNow's multimodal change framework. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: The Cloud Infrastructure model is designed for commissioning or decommissioning Cloud Infrastructure services, not external system integration.
The Unauthorized Change model is triggered by unauthorized change events, not external system integration.
Multimodal Change is a framework for customizing change workflows, not specifically for external system integration.

references: ITSM Fundamentals - Change Management Creation and Scope

source.excerpt: In an out-of-the-box installation, there are several examples available, such as the Change Registration model, which records change requests from an external system without any associated approvals.

questions.question: Which Change Advisory Board (CAB) Workbench features enable collaboration among CAB members? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: The CAB Workbench allows members to schedule in-person meetings and conference calls, facilitating collaboration among Change Advisory Board members. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=65b24dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Creating change task records is done through the Change Request form, not the CAB Workbench specifically.
Automatic risk recalculation is a feature of the risk calculation related link, not the CAB Workbench collaboration features.

source.excerpt: The CAB Workbench can schedule in-person meetings and conference calls.

questions.question: What distinguishes risk conditions from risk assessments in Change Management risk calculation?

options.text: Risk conditions use predefined properties and conditions; risk assessments rely on user-provided information
Risk conditions calculate risk automatically; risk assessments require manual calculation
Risk conditions apply only to emergency changes; risk assessments apply to normal changes
Risk conditions are used before change creation; risk assessments are used after closure

explanation.correct: Risk conditions utilize predefined properties and conditions to calculate a risk value, while risk assessments rely on information provided by the end user to assess a risk value. Both methods can be used independently or in combination, with the highest risk value being chosen. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Both risk conditions and risk assessments require some form of calculation; the difference is in the data source (predefined vs user-provided), not automatic vs manual.
The risk calculation methods apply to all change types, not specifically emergency or normal changes.
Risk calculation occurs during the assessment phase of a change, not before creation or after closure.

references: ITSM Fundamentals - Change Management Creation and Scope

source.excerpt: To determine the risk of a change, there are two methods available. The first is through risk conditions, which utilize predefined properties and conditions to calculate a risk value. The second is through risk assessments, which rely on the information provided by the end user to assess a risk value.

questions.question: In Change Management, what is required to automatically update a change's Schedule tab with actual start and end dates after implementation?

options.text: The change must be in the 'Authorized' state before implementation
The change implementer must manually enter the dates after implementation
The scheduled implementation window must be reached, triggering automatic date capture
A change task of type 'Implementation' must be created and closed

explanation.correct: Once the scheduled implementation window occurs and the change is implemented, the Schedule tab automatically updates with the actual start and end dates. This provides accurate data for reporting and analysis. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: The 'Authorized' state means CAB has approved the change and it's waiting for the scheduled window. Automatic date capture happens when the scheduled window is reached, regardless of prior state.
The Schedule tab automatically captures actual dates when the scheduled implementation window is reached - no manual entry is required.
While change tasks track implementation work, the Schedule tab's automatic date capture is tied to the scheduled window, not task closure.

references: ITSM Fundamentals - Change Management Creation and Scope

source.excerpt: Once the change is implemented, this tab will automatically update with the actual start and end date.

questions.question: A change request has been rejected by CAB. What must happen before the change can be submitted for approval again?

options.text: The change must be canceled and a new change request created
Comments explaining the rejection must be provided, and the change reverts to the New state
The change automatically returns to the Assess state for revision
Emergency changes require no comments; normal changes require supervisor sign-off

explanation.correct: When a change is rejected, comments are necessary to explain why, and the change reverts to its New state. The requester then needs to address the feedback before resubmitting for CAB approval. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=65b24dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: A rejected change does not need to be canceled and recreated. It reverts to the New state where the requester can address feedback and resubmit.
The change does not automatically return to Assess state. It returns to the New state for the requester to address rejection comments.
All rejected changes require comments explaining the rejection, regardless of change type. This is a standard part of the approval workflow.

source.excerpt: If the change is rejected, comments are necessary to explain why, and the change is reverted to its new state.

questions.question: What distinguishes the Emergency Change Advisory Board (ECAB) from the regular CAB?

options.text: ECAB is a subset of CAB that operates under stricter timelines and focuses on minimizing potential risks
ECAB has authority over all emergency changes; CAB only handles normal and standard changes
ECAB requires three approvers while CAB requires only one
ECAB operates during business hours; CAB operates 24/7

explanation.correct: The ECAB is a subset of the CAB specifically responsible for handling emergency changes. Unlike the regular CAB, the ECAB operates under stricter timelines and focuses primarily on minimizing potential risks due to the expedited nature of emergency changes. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=65b24dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Both CAB and ECAB can handle various change types. The ECAB specifically handles emergency changes, but this is about the subset of CAB members focused on urgency, not exclusive authority.
The number of approvers is not what distinguishes ECAB from CAB. The ECAB is distinguished by being a subset focused on emergency changes with stricter timelines.
Operating hours are not what distinguishes ECAB from CAB. ECAB is available on-call for emergency situations rather than having fixed operating hours.

source.excerpt: The Emergency Change Advisory Board, ECAB, is a subset of the CAB responsible for handling emergency changes. Unlike the CAB, the ECAB operates under stricter timelines and focuses primarily on minimizing potential risks.

questions.question: Which scheduling conflicts can the Change Management conflict detection feature identify? (Choose two.)

options.text: A CI is already scheduled at the given date and time
The assigned user has exceeded their maximum change quota for the quarter
The parent CI of the change is within a blackout window
The change model is not approved by the change manager

explanation.correct: Conflict detection identifies scheduling conflicts including when a CI is already scheduled at the given date and time, and when a parent or child CI falls within a blackout window. These conflicts can be reviewed in the conflict calendar. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: User change quotas are not detected by the conflict detection feature. Conflict detection focuses on CI scheduling conflicts, blackout windows, and resource availability.
Change model approval status is not a scheduling conflict detected by the conflict detection feature. This is a separate approval workflow concern.

references: ITSM Fundamentals - Change Management Creation and Scope

source.excerpt: These conflicts may arise if the CIs are already scheduled at the given date and time, if a parent or child of the configuration item is already scheduled, or if the configuration item parent or child falls outside the maintenance window. Perhaps the configuration item, its parent, or its child may be within a blackout window.

questions.question: Which ITIL role enables a user to create, update, and close changes and configuration items, and is most suitable for a support group responsible for implementing changes?

explanation.correct: The ITIL role is crucial for anyone in a support group responsible for implementing changes. This role enables users to create, update, and close changes and configuration items. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: The change_manager role oversees schedules, change approval policies, and standard change proposals - it is not the role for day-to-day change implementation by support groups.
The itil_admin role can create, update, close, and delete changes and associated records, and is most suitable for a team lead, not a support group implementing changes.
change_coordinator is not a standard ITIL role in ServiceNow Change Management. The standard roles are itil, itil_admin, and change_manager.

references: ITSM Fundamentals - Change Management Creation and Scope

source.excerpt: The ITIL role is crucial for anyone in a support group responsible for implementing changes. This role enables users to create, update, and close change and configuration items.
